newsitem.title: USA: Short people take heart -- dwarf mice live longer.
newsitem.headline: Short people take heart -- dwarf mice live longer.

text.p: Living longer may be the best revenge for short people, a researcher studying the longer lifespans of rare dwarf mice said on Wednesday.
The as-yet unpublished study of the tiny breed of mouse, which are about one-third the size of normal-sized laboratory mice, found that they live up to twice as long as their larger cousins.

"It's very difficult to directly relate this research to humans," University of North Dakota physiologist Holly Brown-Borg warned in an interview. "But a study in the early 1990s of 350 to 400 men found shorter men lived about five years longer than taller, heavier men."
She noted that smaller breeds of dogs and horses also tend to live longer.

The reason, Brown-Borg explained, is that larger amounts of the hormones excreted by the pituitary gland that help determine body size and regulate the metabolic rate and immune system also accelerate the ageing process.

The research could have repercussions in the burgeoning field of hormone therapy, where short-statured children are given growth hormone supplements to boost height. Older people or people ill with the wasting symptoms of AIDS whose muscles are atrophying are also given hormones to build muscle mass.

The rare dwarf mouse, discovered 30 years ago, does not produce the three hormones. Compared to the 22-month lifespan of its normal-sized cousins, male dwarf mice eating a similar diet lived almost a year longer and females 15 months longer, according to the research, much of which was done at Southern Illinois University in Carbondale.
One drawback for the dwarf mice lacking the hormone prolactin was that tests on individual cells found their immune systems were slower to respond to germs.
Brown-Borg published a letter in the British journal Nature outlining her research and planned to submit a full paper on her work to a scientific journal.
